The Green humphead parrotfish Bolbometopon muricatum is among the largest herbivorous fishes inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reefs, with a maximum recorded total length of 130 cm [Li = 130 cm] according to extensive underwater visual surveys conducted across the Great Barrier Reef and the Coral Triangle. This species exhibits a slow, determinate growth trajectory typical of large-bodied scarids, and field studies indicate that individuals can live for approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] at the average annual water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law curve derived from a large sample of commercially landed specimens, yielding an estimated ultimate wet weight of 35,000 grams [Wwi = 35,000 grams] for an individual attaining the asymptotic length. These enormous adults, which can exceed 50 kilograms, play a critical ecological role as bioeroders, actively excavating the carbonate substrate as they feed on endolithic algae and live coral polyps. Their conspicuous feeding scars, left behind on the reef framework, contribute substantially to the production of fine sediment in lagoon and back-reef environments.

Reproductive biology in Bolbometopon muricatum remains relatively understudied compared to smaller parrotfish species, but recent histological analyses of gonadal tissue from specimens collected at a site in Papua New Guinea provide valuable insights. Sexual maturation occurs when individuals achieve a total length of 60 cm [Lp = 60 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 3,508 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,508 grams] based on the length-weight relationship established for the population. Fish at this stage typically exhibit fully differentiated gonadal architecture, though initial gametogenesis may begin slightly earlier in faster-growing individuals. The capacity to reproduce is thus attained only after a prolonged juvenile phase lasting several years, during which the fish must accumulate substantial somatic reserves before directing energy toward gamete production. This delayed maturation pattern is consistent with a life-history strategy optimized for high adult survivorship and repeated, multi-year spawning events.

At the very beginning of the life cycle, the minute size of newly hatched propagules presents a stark contrast to the massive adult dimensions. Based on an egg diameter of 0.75 mm measured in a related chaetodontid species, the wet weight at birth for Bolbometopon muricatum is estimated at only 0.00022 grams [Wwb = 0.00022 grams], reflecting the small volume of the yolk-laden egg at the moment of chorion rupture. The fertilised ovum drifts as a pelagic egg in the water column before hatching into a lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva that relies entirely on endogenous reserves during its first days of development. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening and is a critical bottleneck in the early life history, as larvae must successfully capture suitable planktonic prey to avoid starvation. The tiny mass of the newly emerged individual underscores the immense potential for mortality during the early pelagic larval phase, a period during which predators, starvation, and physical transport all impose heavy selective pressures.

Under the stable thermal conditions of tropical reef waters, maintained at approximately 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the reproductive physiology of this species follows a predictable seasonal pattern. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated as the percentage of total body mass accounted for by ovarian tissue, reached a mean peak of 8% [GSI = 8%] during the height of the spawning season at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. Spawning occurs as two distinct spawning episodes per year [F_R_i = two distinct spawning episodes per year]. The annual reproductive output is therefore distributed across multiple batches, which may enhance larval survival by spreading the risk of encountering unfavorable oceanographic conditions. This iteroparous, batch-spawning mode is widely observed among large-bodied scarids in equatorial reef ecosystems.

The maximum longevity of approximately 27 years [am = approximately 27 years] recorded for this species, estimated from otolith increment analysis, places it among the longer-lived members of the family Scaridae at a temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with the thermal regime of their tropical habitat at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], allows for many repeated spawning opportunities across the adult years, theoretically enabling a single female to produce millions of eggs over her lifetime. The combination of a high adult survival rate and moderate annual fecundity suggests that population resilience in Bolbometopon muricatum depends heavily on the protection of large, old individuals that contribute disproportionately to larval supply over many years. Recent declines in abundance across parts of its range, driven by targeted spear fishing and habitat degradation, have raised concerns about the erosion of this demographic buffer. Conservation measures such as marine protected areas and size limits are increasingly advocated to safeguard the remaining reproductively valuable adults before local populations reach critically low densities. Despite its formidable size, this species exhibits a slow life history, and recovery from overexploitation may require several decades under optimal conditions, highlighting the need for precautionary management strategies that account for the time necessary to rebuild spawning biomass and restore the functional role of these large bioeroders on coral reefs.
